/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.headline: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.excerpt: Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned. Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems. Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations. Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].” The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028.
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.trail: Johan Rockström, one of world’s leading climate experts, says slowing down scientific work puts cooperation at risk

/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.headline: ‘Risk multiplier’: super El Niño looms over Cop31 as climate pattern fuels global disasters
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.excerpt: If the galloping pace of the climate crisis isn’t enough to spur countries to act at UN climate talks under way in Turkey, there is another major threat heightening its havoc: the strongest El Niño event in at least 1,000 years. The “jaw-dropping” El Niño, a naturally recurring phenomenon where the eastern Pacific heats up every few years with temporary but global implications, has provided added urgency to wrangling at the Cop31 summit over climate funding for vulnerable countries that are having to scramble to respond. Already, warping global weather patterns have fuelled huge wildfires and crop failures in Indonesia, coastal inundation in the US, severe drought in Sudan and severe flooding in countries including Ecuador and Somalia. “We are supercharging our weather and El Niño will be a risk multiplier,” said Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the World Meteorological Organization. Drought has ravaged the Marshall Islands, a small Pacific atoll country that relies heavily on rainfall for its water. “It’s a compounding crisis, we are trying to prepare but the drought has already hit and it’s on top of having to deal with rising seas that threaten our homes and drinking water,” said Kathy Jetn̄il-Kijiner, climate envoy for the Marshall Islands, which has declared a state of emergency. Last year, wealthy countries agreed to triple the amount of adaptation finance to poorer countries most vulnerable to floods, heatwaves, wildfires and other damaging climate impacts.
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.trail: Strongest El Niño in centuries adds urgency to UN climate talks as vulnerable countries face ‘compounding’ crises

/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.headline: ‘You cannot build peace on a burning planet,’ UN chief tells Cop31 in farewell speech
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.excerpt: Tackling the climate crisis is central to all of human life and must be at the forefront of global governance, the outgoing UN secretary general has said in an emotional farewell address at the Cop31 climate summit. “You cannot build peace on a burning planet,” António Guterres said at his final climate press conference as secretary general on Friday. “You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it. You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends.” Guterres has been the most forthright secretary general yet on the subject of the climate, returning to it again and again to castigate fossil fuel companies and recalcitrant governments. He leaves office at the end of December and his successor is still unknown after Donald Trump tried to interject his preferred choices into the process. There are widespread fears that the next incumbent will downplay the climate crisis in favour of other issues. In a clear message to his successor, Guterres spelled out why the UN must continue to place the climate at the top of the global agenda. “Climate change does not stay in its lane,” he said. “It drives anger and displacement around the world. It wipes out development gains built over decades. It pushes countries deeper into deficit. It aggravates competition for land and water. “It fuels instability. And increasingly, it threatens the very existence of communities and countries.
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.trail: António Guterres says climate action central to every aspect of UN’s work, as leaders depart Cop31 and talks go on

/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.headline: California governor Gavin Newsom endorses global fossil fuel phaseout
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.excerpt: The leader of the world’s fourth-biggest economy, California governor Gavin Newsom, has explicitly endorsed a global phaseout of the fossil fuels that drive climate breakdown. Newsom said that California is “100%” behind the efforts of the so-called Santa Marta coalition, a group of more than 50 countries that includes many of the world’s largest economies, to transition away from oil, gas and coal toward solar, wind, batteries and other non-carbon energy sources. Speaking at the Cop31 UN climate summit on Thursday, Newsom said: “When you have a product that is obviously superior, which clean energy is for the climate and the economy, why wouldn’t you make that shift as quickly as possible?” As the head of America’s most populous and economically powerful state, Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the Trump administration continues to boycott. Newsom, a Democrat, is widely expected to run for president in 2028. His statement raises the possibility that the US, the world’s biggest economy and largest historical emitter of planet-warming gases, could join the Santa Marta coalition if he wins the presidency two years from now. More than 80 countries wanted last year’s COP30 to begin to develop a global “roadmap” to phase out fossil fuels. A handful of petrostates led by Saudi Arabia blocked that effort, relying on the disputed notion that decisions at UN climate summits can only be made by consensus.
/environment/2026/nov/21/climate-talks-s.trail: Newsom is the most prominent US politician at Cop31, a process the Trump administration continues to boycott

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.headline: New Bradford railway station will ‘transform travel across the north’
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.excerpt: A new railway station will be built in Bradford to “transform how people travel across the north”, the government has announced. The station will be at the heart of the Northern Powerhouse Rail (NPR) scheme, built on the current Bradford Interchange site but allowing through trains between Leeds and Manchester. With the promise of more frequent and faster services, it is expected to support new homes and jobs for the West Yorkshire city, located alongside its Southern Gateway regeneration project and connecting to the proposed tram to Leeds. Approval of the station, which is expected to be built by the mid-2030s, has been regarded by northern leaders as a critical sign of political commitment to improving rail links across the north, after long delays in delivering pledged upgrades. The Department for Transport said that NPR would allow a “turn-up-and-go railway” for passengers from Bradford, with sufficiently frequent trains running across the north for people not to need to check timetables. The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “Today marks an important milestone for Bradford with a brand-new station that will transform how people travel across the north.” The new station, along with the proposed West Yorkshire mass transit network – better known as the Leeds tram – will bring more than £1bn in economic benefits, according to Bradford council.

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.headline: Rebellion review – story of Bradford 12 revisits Britain’s ugly racist past
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.excerpt: This fierce film from socialist film-makers Ken Fero and Tariq Mehmood gives us the story and the context of the Bradford 12. Twelve south Asian members of the United Black Youth League in 1981 were arrested on a charge of conspiracy to cause explosions for possessing dozens of molotov cocktails – milk bottles filled with petrol, with a rag through the lid – allegedly for throwing at the police. To the intense irritation of the British authorities, a mixed-race jury acquitted them, accepting their argument that it was in self-defence (and that the items themselves were closer to fireworks than bombs), because black and Asian communities were routinely and systematically attacked by skinheads and racists whose activities were shrugged at by the powers that be. It is a reminder of a particularly ugly, squalid, bigoted and mediocre era in British public life, when Margaret Thatcher, just before becoming prime minister, tried to siphon off some of the far-right National Front’s political energy by declaring that people felt “swamped” by immigrants, the most earsplittingly loud dog whistle in Tory history.
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.trail: Ken Fero and Tariq Mehmood’s documentary recalls the fight against racism in 1980s Britain – even if its account of solidarity has a notable omission

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.headline: ‘It smelled like dead people’: the plan to tackle England’s illegal waste problem
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.excerpt: “There were parents dropping their children off and then heaving from the smell,” says Liz Thompson, 45, who runs Blessings Nursery in Bradford, West Yorkshire. During the recent heatwaves, the smell from an illegal waste dump on Midland Road, just metres from the nursery, became so unbearable that staff had to keep the doors and windows shut and the children couldn’t play outside. “It smelled like dead people, like really bad rotten food. It was horrible,” she says. The smell, which lingered for weeks, started to impact Thompson’s business, with prospective parents put off from enrolling their children at the nursery. “It was embarrassing,” she says. The situation Thompson faced is far from a one-off. The Environment Agency received 10,238 reports of suspected waste crime in England in 2025. Yorkshire is a particular hotspot, with a new heatmap showing 1,068 reports in 2025, second only to the West Midlands, where a record 1,542 reports of waste crime were filed. These figures are probably underestimated, with just 27% of waste crimes thought to be reported. It’s a problem that particularly exercises the public and it’s striking that in one of his first moves as prime minister, Andy Burnham visited the Midland Road waste dump, declaring that the “days of making easy money out of waste are over”. The dump, which first came on to Bradford Council and the Environment Agency’s radar in June after reports of foul smells, had been building for months.
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/man-charged-with-at.trail: Andy Burnham has announced a crackdown, but doubts remain over authorities’ ability to take on organised crime

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.headline: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing dinghy in Channel
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.excerpt: The far-right agitator Daniel Thomas has been sentenced to 15 months in jail after slashing a dinghy that had been carrying asylum seekers in the Channel. Judge Newton-Price KC described Thomas as a “publicity seeker” who had interfered with the work of law enforcement officers and lifesavers. The judge said: “This offence amounted to a flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption of the legitimate activities of the border force, the coastguard and RNLI [Royal National Lifeboat Institution] volunteers.” He added: “Those organisations perform essential roles in policing the maritime border. They do necessary, highly sensitive and very difficult jobs. Their work should not be interrupted by a publicity seeker slashing with a knife at a boat that they were trying to recover.” Thomas, the founder of the anti-migration group Patriot Platform, had taken a boat out into the Channel and observed asylum seekers in a dinghy being assisted by the RNLI, Border Force and French coastguard on 22 September. He asked for his boat to be steered towards the rigid-hulled inflatable boat, and armed himself with a knife as rescue crews approached the dinghy and a French man boarded it. Newton-Price said Thomas had slashed the boat about eight times and his actions would have alarmed anyone close at hand. The judge said the fact the incident was livestreamed meant there must have been a “high degree of planning or premeditation”.
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.trail: Thomas sentenced to 15 months after admitting to criminal damage to vessel that had been carrying asylum seekers

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.headline: Torture survivors may have been sent to Sussex asylum camp unlawfully, documentary reveals
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.excerpt: Asylum seekers accommodated at a controversial military base in East Sussex have been subjected to inadequate welfare checks, and torture survivors may have been placed there unlawfully, an undercover documentary for ITV has revealed. Mass accommodation sites are central to the government’s plan to end the use of hotels to house asylum seekers. For the documentary, Inside The Asylum Camp, ITV’s undercover reporter got a job as a welfare officer at Crowborough and covertly filmed inside the former military training camp. The documentary claims that poor screening and welfare checks are having serious consequences for some of the asylum seekers. This May, the high court ruled that a Home Office policy change forcing torture survivors to share rooms was unlawful. The accommodation at Crowborough is in large dormitories. The Home Office’s decision to accommodate asylum seekers on two former military sites – Crowborough, and Wethersfield in Essex – has triggered opposition from local residents. Plans to use three other sites – Bicester, Barnham and Linton-on-Ouse – have caused a similar outcry, mostly around fears about asylum seekers causing a rise in violent crime. However, very low levels of even minor crimes have been recorded by police at Wethersfield and Crowborough among asylum seekers at the two camps. The Crowborough site is run by Clearsprings Ready Homes.
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.trail: Undercover ITV report also shows inadequate welfare checks at ex-military base run by firm of asylum camp billionaire Graham King

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.headline: Tory and Reform politicians clash over migration as asylum centre approved
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.excerpt: Senior Tory and Reform politicians have clashed over immigration policy in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington after the government approved plans to convert a defence site into accommodation for asylum seekers. Zia Yusuf and Chris Philp raised their voices and spoke over each other in front of TV cameras and local people for more than three minutes. Yusuf urged his fellow home affairs spokesperson to apologise for his record as a minister. Philp said they should instead “stand in solidarity with residents” and Yusuf should “read the room”. The clash came hours after villagers said they would launch a legal challenge to plans to house more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers near them. It emerged on Thursday that Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, had approved full planning permission, a decision welcomed by the Home Office, which wants to end the use of asylum hotels. In their clash, Yusuf said: “Chris, would you like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into the country illegally?” Philp, who served as an immigration minister, said: “That is disingenuous, Zia, as usual … I hope today we can stand in solidarity with the residents.

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.headline: Home Office denies British baby living in Thailand chance to meet great-grandfather in UK
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.excerpt: The Home Office has denied a great-grandfather from Lancashire the chance of meeting his five-month-old British great-grandson, who lives abroad. William Cross was born in Thailand on 30 April to parents Matthew Cross, 31, who is from Burnley in Lancashire, and Khin Thant Zin, known as Jue Jue, also 31, a refugee who fled persecution in Myanmar to Thailand. The family live on the island of Koh Tao, famous for its diving schools and a centre for turtle conservation. It is a popular tourism spot and Cross, a mechanical engineer, opened a steakhouse restaurant there 15 months ago. He met Zin on the island and the couple are now engaged. She works in the restaurant managing social media and human resources. Cross’s parents have visited the family in Thailand and have met their grandson. But William’s great-grandfather George Kerr, 74, who lives in Clayton-le-Moors in Lancashire, has multiple health problems and so is unable to fly out to Thailand to meet the baby. Instead, a large family gathering was planned in Burnley for Christmas. Cross said: “My grandfather suffers from ill health and sadly he is unable to travel. He and I have been extremely close all my life and I’m desperate for him to meet his [great] grandchild.” The family have just signed a lease on a new home and have bought some land on the island for later development. They assumed that organising a short trip to the UK for a family Christmas would be straightforward.
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.trail: British father would like to take his family to Lancashire to see ill relative but officials refused visa for his partner, a refugee from Myanmar

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.headline: UK law could deny Fayed accusers recognition as victims of human trafficking
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.excerpt: Survivors of sexual violence could wrongly be denied recognition as victims of human trafficking under credibility tests in a new UK law, the independent anti-slavery commissioner has warned. Eleanor Lyons said the measures in the immigration and asylum bill were fundamentally unfair and could lead to many more victims of slavery and trafficking, including those allegedly abused by Mohamed Al Fayed, being denied support. Under the legislation, Home Office officials must regard any delay to making a claim of modern day slavery or human trafficking as damaging to their credibility. Any inaccuracy, inconsistency or omission in a person’s account, as well as any striking similarity to a claim made by someone else, must also be viewed as reasons for disbelief. Lyons said the credibility tests would harm survivors of sexual violence who often suffered memory loss as a result of their trauma. Many were also reluctant to come forward to disclose their exploitation due to fear of reprisals by their abusers, she added. “They are basically saying to victims, if you don’t come forward in a timely fashion not yet defined, if there are inconsistencies in your account, and if there are similarities between exploitation and [those of] others, the Home Office decision-maker must question your credibility,” Lyons said.
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/suffolk-village-vot.trail: ‘Unfair’ immigration and asylum bill could fail to support sexual violence survivors, anti-slavery commissioner says

/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/21/peter-fluck-ca.headline: Sarah’s Channel: a beauty blogger ignores the end of the world in this increasingly relatable spoof
/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/21/peter-fluck-ca.excerpt: For most of her career, Australian actor and comedian Claudia O’Doherty has played on her adorable persona in the whimsical worlds of Bluey, Our Flag Means Death and Love, among others. She’s all big eyes and bangs, stealing scenes and hearts. But, as anyone who saw surprise hit Maddie’s Secret would know, O’Doherty is supremely satisfying as a villain. In John Early’s surreal yet oddly moving tale of a female food influencer’s battle with an eating disorder, O’Doherty broke bad as Maddie’s nemesis, Emily. Unlike her roles as lovable underdog, Emily weaponises her sexuality through calorific “dude food” and psychologically annihilates anyone who dares threaten her umami-infused reign. For many, Maddie’s Secret was the first time they’d seen O’Doherty as an antagonist. But it wasn’t the first time she played a girl next door twisted into a villain by the punishing world around her and online. In 2019, O’Doherty starred as the beauty blogger Sarah in the ABC web series Sarah’s Channel. Across five five-minute episodes (and a blooper reel) we follow Sarah as she shows off her room, her favourite products, her wellness routine and even a potential boyfriend. Although, as soon as she introduces her first product, holding it against her palm like a well trained content creator, it’s clear this isn’t going to be a normal “get ready with me” (GRWM).

/sport/2026/nov/21/england-new-zealand-n.headline: Fading Beauden Barrett a painful symbol of All Blacks’ joyless decline
/sport/2026/nov/21/england-new-zealand-n.excerpt: If their punishment last week was to be told in no uncertain terms that they had let the country down, what awaits the All Blacks after this? Public humiliation? Exile? A firing squad at dawn? That New Zealand followed head coach Dave Rennie’s rebuke with their worst Twickenham performance of the professional era and a record defeat by England suggests such criticism monumentally backfired. Perhaps it is wise to remember it is only a game, Dave. For what made the very best All Blacks sides so impressive was that they always looked like they were having fun. That they would showcase the most mesmerising skills and do so with a smile on their faces took the breath away and added to the allure. This rabble did not look like they were having much fun out there. With hindsight, it is clear what Rennie was trying to do, but his comments say much about the All Blacks’ problems. As the NRL grows in popularity, rugby union is just not the religion it once was. When Rennie apologises he does so to an increasingly apathetic New Zealand public. Those of us here at Twickenham 12 months ago wondered if New Zealand’s dismal performance was an aberration. Never before had the All Blacks been so insipid and it was a defeat that cost Scott Robertson his job. This was a good deal worse. If you want to hit the All Blacks where it hurts, you question their ball handling skills. Here, they were shocking, hesitant in possession. Rabbits in headlights.

This week Erasmus was banned for six matches for questioning whether officials are match-fixing and suggested they had “manipulated the game”, comments widely perceived as a cynical attempt to exert pressure on officials in the Springboks’ forthcoming matches. The resurfacing of the Australia cricket team’s use of sandpaper in 2018, meanwhile, has brought back into focus how low another elite sporting side were willing to stoop in pursuit of victory. “There’s a line,” the England captain said. “I don’t believe in the metric of win at all costs because, depending on what that cost is, it can be extremely damaging. Integrity is really important. I’m Christian as well, so there are certain things which I wouldn’t do, or [positions] I wouldn’t put myself in. There’s a passage in the Bible that says something along the lines of ‘what does it gain for a man to gain the world but lose his soul?’. Part of that is why I don’t believe in that kind of thing.

/sport/2026/nov/21/england-new-zealand-n.headline: England braced for All Black-lash in the ultimate test of their mini-upturn
/sport/2026/nov/21/england-new-zealand-n.excerpt: From the Bay of Islands on the northern tip of New Zealand to Invercargill in the deep south, there is rare unanimity this week. Back in the day there would be parochial arguments about, say, the ratio of Aucklanders to Cantabrians in the starting XV. This time there is nationwide recognition that absolutely nothing matters beyond a bounce-back win for the boys in black on Saturday. It is the inevitable upshot of last weekend’s seismic defeat by Wales, a result that prompted Dave Rennie, the head coach, to admit his reshuffled team had “let ourselves and our country down”. The former All Black scrum-half Justin Marshall went a step further. “We were arrogant enough to think that we could make those changes and still protect our history, and now look what’s happened,” a wounded Marshall told the GBRNRZ podcast. And even in this noisiest of rugby weeks, the New Zealand teamsheet speaks loudest. Injuries aside this is the strongest selection these touring All Blacks could have fielded and the Kiwi desire for atonement is almost tangible. “They’ve got 500 more caps this week,” said Steve Borthwick, primed for a significant Black-lash. “It’s a very different proposition of a team.” But hang on. England’s lineup for this ultimate test of their latest mini-upturn is also pretty much their best current squad, give or take the injured Manny Feyi-Waboso and Alex Mitchell and which of the Curry twins is available.

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/british-man-recalls.headline: British man fined €3,000 for causing two-year-old son’s death in Cyprus
/uk-news/2026/nov/21/british-man-recalls.excerpt: A British man has been fined €3,000 (£2,500) after his two-year-old son fell 10 metres (33ft) to his death from the fourth-floor window of a hotel in Cyprus. Joshua Foster thought the window was closed when he approached it with the boy to show him the view of a waterpark and “lost control” of him, the court previously heard. The 37-year-old appeared at Paphos district court on Friday for sentencing having pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. In emotional scenes at the court, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident on 12 July, the first day of the family’s holiday in Cyprus, as a “tragic event”. “Jail is not appropriate,” the judge said, telling the courtroom that as there was “clearly no intent to kill” she had decided against a custodial sentence and would instead order Foster to pay the fine. The Essex-born auditor, who had previously appeared in court visibly distraught, struggled to hold back tears as the sentence was handed down. As it dawned that the case was finally over, he hugged his lawyer before telling reporters: “Thank you for your support. I’m looking forward to going home and being with my wife and daughter.” The light sentence – the minimum for the charge – meant Foster could retrieve his passport and other documents he had been forced to surrender.

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/british-man-recalls.excerpt: A British man has pleaded guilty to “recklessly” causing the death of his son, 10 weeks after the toddler fell from a fourth-floor hotel window in Cyprus. Josh Foster, 37, who appeared before the district court of Paphos on Tuesday, accepted the charge of causing the accident through a “rash, reckless and dangerous act” on the first day of a family holiday near Paphos on 12 July. The case was adjourned until 5 October, when the judge ordered the man to return for sentencing. Under the maximum penalty he could face up to four years in prison. Explaining his client’s decision to enter the plea, the defence lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said the alternative was the prospect of prolonged criminal proceedings. If he had contested the charge, a series of hearings would have ensued, forcing the father to repeatedly confront the circumstances of the two-year-old’s death. His client had broken down inconsolably when he appeared in the same courtroom to be formally charged in July. “[A trial] would be disturbing for him, for his family,” said Alexandrou, emphasising that the Briton, his wife and other relatives were still processing the grief of their “unimaginable loss”. “In order to end this story he accepted [the accusation],” he said, adding the defence would present mitigating factors in an attempt to secure a lenient verdict. “If the maximum sentence were imposed, the defence would appeal.

/uk-news/2026/nov/21/british-man-recalls.excerpt: A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast. The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia. Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20. A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot. International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials. Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”. The Isin, capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.

/us-news/2026/nov/21/california-arrests-.headline: Russian national charged with spying on Silicon Valley tech and defense firm
/us-news/2026/nov/21/california-arrests-.excerpt: The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia. On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents. According to officials, D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully this summer after being recruited by co-conspirators through Telegram. His alleged mission was to “carry out clandestine assignments targeting employees of a large technology and defense company with an office in Palo Alto, California”, the justice department said, without identifying the company or the alleged co-conspirators. Bloomberg reported that the company in question was Palantir Technologies, citing an unnamed source familiar with the matter. The firm has a large office in Palo Alto. The department added that D’iu had reportedly received instructions, equipment and financial support from the co-conspirators, who told him that his work was for “the Motherland”. They also allegedly instructed him to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine. The Russian embassy was contacted for comment.

/us-news/2026/nov/21/california-arrests-.headline: FBI raids and a recycling firm: how a promising US mayor wound up at the center of a bribery scandal
/us-news/2026/nov/21/california-arrests-.excerpt: Two years ago, residents of Oakland, California, woke up to a shocking scene: their mayor’s home was being raided by the FBI. Agents were seen carrying dozens of boxes from the hilltop home of Sheng Thao, the city’s 38-year-old leader, as part of an investigation constituents would later learn alleged her participation in a pay-to-play scheme with the city’s recycling contractor. It was a stunning moment for Thao, who was elected to lead the Bay Area city in 2022 and was once seen as a promising young mayor in a city that has long grappled with economic inequality and a reputation for violent crime. Her story of growing up in a refugee family and overcoming domestic violence and homelessness to become the first person of Hmong descent to run a major US city resonated with residents confronting questions about equity and representation that came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, and made her the subject of glowing media profiles. As mayor, Thao revived the city’s Ceasefire violence-reduction strategy and brought in a much-needed infusion of revenue through the sale of the Oakland Coliseum sports complex. But her tenure was far from smooth. At the time of the raid she was already facing a heated recall campaign grounded in her perceived failure to address the city’s mounting public safety and homelessness crises – one that would see her ousted from office in November 2024.

/us-news/2026/nov/21/california-arrests-.excerpt: Nima Momeni, the man convicted of murdering Cash App founder Bob Lee, has been sentenced to 16 years to life. Momeni, 42, has been in San Francisco’s county jail since late April of 2023, after he was arrested in connection with the stabbing death of Lee, who had created the mobile payment service and was serving as the chief product officer of the cryptocurrency MobileCoin at the time of his death. Family members of both men and Momeni himself spoke during the sentencing hearing, SFGate reports. Lee’s daughter, Scout Lee, who was 14 when her father was killed, told the judge her world was “shattered” after her father was killed. “Mr Momeni, you didn’t just take my dad that day,” Scout said. “You took my best friend.” Momeni’s mother, Mahnaz Tayarani, implored the judge to look beyond her son’s crime and base his sentence on the totality of her son’s life. “I am here because I love my son,” Tayarani said. “A person’s life can hold more than the worst moment of his life. Nima is not perfect. No human being is.” Momeni, clad in an orange jail uniform, told the judge: “It was never my intention to see anyone hurt or suffer … I’m truly sorry,” he said. Momeni’s sentencing marks the end of a case that shocked those in the highest echelons of the US tech industry.

That year, Nicole Brown Simpson and Goldman were found stabbed to death outside her home in Los Angeles. The American professional football player and actor, OJ Simpson, was suspected in the killings. Simpson’s prosecution gained international attention and became a media spectacle, being deemed the “trial of the century”. Simpson was acquitted by a jury in 1995 after a lengthy trial. The Los Angeles police department, which investigated the case, had a long history of racism. Simpson’s attorneys pointed to the racist policing practices and the department’s handling of key evidence, helping them secure the acquittal. Simpson was later held liable for the deaths by a jury in a civil case.
